profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CyrusOne cluster sits in the Cincinnati metro area, spanning Cincinnati, Lebanon, and Butler and Warren Counties in Ohio and Florence, Kentucky just across the Ohio River. This is CyrusOne home market: Wikipedia coverage states Cincinnati Bell purchased CyrusOne for 525 million dollars in 2010 and later divested its remaining stake in 2015 after the company IPO in 2013. CyrusOne was originally founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten. The company was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CIN2 sits at 229 West 7th Street in downtown Cincinnati with 11 MW of published IT capacity across roughly 144,000 square feet of technical space. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 11 MW supports approximately 275 racks; at a more modest 10 kW per rack, a figure more typical of colocation mixed workloads, the same power budget reaches around 1,100 racks. Those are assumptions about rack density, not operator claims. The 144,000 square feet of technical space is generous relative to 11 MW, which suggests the floor plan was designed for lower-density compute rather than the high-kilowatt-per-rack configurations that GPU clusters require today.

The certifications qualify this campus to host regulated workloads. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment card data. HIPAA qualifies it for protected health information. ISO 27001 certifies a formal information security management system. FISMA qualifies it for certain federal information systems. SSAE 16 Type II documents that audited controls operated effectively over a defined period. Together they position CIN2 for compliance-sensitive enterprise work rather than signaling any particular AI infrastructure orientation.

Among the 76 facilities this site has mapped in Ohio, only two have published a megawatt figure at all, and CIN2 is ranked second of those two, accounting for 11 of the 23 total published megawatts in the state. That makes it one of the more legible campuses in Ohio by this metric, but the picture is incomplete because most mapped Ohio facilities publish no capacity figure. Whether CIN2's 11 MW is material to AI scaling depends on a buyer's density requirements, and at current GPU cluster power draws the published capacity is modest rather than large.
